title: Archaeologists discover eerie 'sand body' at Sutton Hoo
excerpt: A shadow from England's distant past has emerged at Sutton Hoo. Archaeologists have uncovered an eerie 'sand body' - the ghostly outline of a person who died around 1,400 years ago.
content:
A shadow from England’s distant past has emerged at Sutton Hoo.

Archaeologists excavating the famous Anglo-Saxon burial ground in Suffolk have uncovered an eerie ‘sand body’ – the ghostly outline of a person who died around 1,400 years ago.

Their flesh and bones have long since vanished, but they left a human-shaped imprint in the sand.

The remarkable discovery was made during new excavations at the internationally renowned site near Woodbridge, where some of Britain's most important early medieval treasures have been found.

Angus Wainwright, archaeologist at the National Trust, said: ‘These were burials where the bodies and bones had dissolved away in the acid soil, replaced by hard sand which held the form of the person not unlike some of the bodies at Pompeii.

‘It was certainly a high point of this latest dig, to find another of these bodies in the Garden Field cemetery.’

Archaeologists excavating the famous site uncovered an eerie ‘sand body’ – the ghostly outline of a person who died around 1,400 years ago

As the corpse decomposed, chemical reactions caused the surrounding sand to harden and preserve the person's shape

Experts believe the individual's remains gradually dissolved in Sutton Hoo's highly acidic soil over the centuries.

Yet as the corpse decomposed, chemical reactions caused the surrounding sand to harden and preserve the person's shape.

The result is a haunting human silhouette that appears to freeze a long-dead individual in time.

Alongside the burial were several grave goods including beads, tweezers, a knife and a brooch, offering fascinating glimpses into the life and identity of the person laid to rest there.

Directly underneath the sand body, the team also found evidence that a second person may have been buried in the same grave.

‘Until now archaeologists have focused on the royal burial mounds,’ Mr Wainwright said.

‘Yet these mounds stood in a landscape of significance to the Saxon kings, as well as one familiar to the everyday East Anglians who lived in the villages and farms of the river valley.

‘This excavation moves the focus to these people and their ancestors and descendants.’

The sand body was uncovered during excavations filmed by Time Team, which recently returned to Sutton Hoo for a new project in partnership with the National Trust.

This was the main trench that was opened up by the team during the dig.The sand body was uncovered during excavations filmed by Time Team, which recently returned to Sutton Hoo for a new project in partnership with the National Trust

Archaeologists also uncovered the Byzantine Bromeswell Bucket, a lavish copper-alloy vessel believed to date from the sixth century

The Sutton Hoo sand body has drawn comparisons with the famous victims of Pompeii, the Roman city destroyed when Mount Vesuvius erupted in AD79.

Although the two phenomena were created in very different ways, both preserve haunting impressions of people long after their remains disappeared.

At Pompeii, dead bodies were covered in layers of volcanic ash before decomposing, leaving behind hollow spaces.

In the 19th century, excavators began injecting plaster into these voids, creating the striking casts that famously capture victims in their final moments.

The casts revealed remarkably detailed impressions of the dead, preserving everything from facial expressions and hairstyles to the folds of clothing and even sandals.

While the Sutton Hoo burials lack the dramatic poses seen at Pompeii, they are similarly rare because they preserve the shape of a person despite the body itself having almost entirely vanished.

Researchers hope further analysis of the grave may reveal clues about the person's age, status and relationship to the second individual buried alongside them.

The Sutton Hoo sand body has drawn comparisons with the famous victims of Pompeii (pictured) 

The site is best known for the spectacular ship burial discovered in 1939, thought to have belonged to an elite ruler, possibly King Raedwald of East Anglia.

As well as the celebrated ship burial, archaeologists have unearthed an iconic helmet, gold jewellery, weapons, coins, gaming pieces and horse burials.

Among Sutton Hoo's more unusual discoveries is the so-called Byzantine Bromeswell Bucket, a lavish copper-alloy vessel believed to date from the sixth century.

Decorated with a hunting scene featuring North African warriors, the bucket is one of the clearest pieces of evidence that the people buried at Sutton Hoo had access to luxury goods from far beyond Britain's shores.

Archaeologists found it had been reused as a cremation vessel containing human remains, including parts of a talus (ankle bone) and fragments of a skull vault (the upper part of the skull that protects the brain), as well as the remains of an animal.

They have since been analysed by specialists to understand the cremation process and determine what was on the funeral pyre.

Horses were often included on early Anglo-Saxon cremation pyres as a sign of status, and the animal bones indicate they belong to an animal larger than a pig.

Dr Helen Geake, Time Team Anglo-Saxon specialist, said: ‘One of the biggest mysteries about the incredible burials in the Sutton Hoo mound cemetery has always been why and when they chose this particular place? That’s what we’ve been trying to find out, together with the National Trust.

‘We were thrilled to finally locate and excavate the burial contained within the Byzantine Bromeswell Bucket and to set it in context – although there are still many questions to answer.

‘There is still much to discover about this iconic site.’
